note_tweet.text:
Utilities are rushing to add supply for an unprecedented wave of new large loads. Many now let large customers bring their own capacity, so new load connects sooner and existing customers are protected from rate impacts. Bring-your-own-capacity (BYOC) rules have rapidly gone from novelty to norm and are now the fastest path to reliable grid power.

Firma Power is the Bring Your Own Capacity company. We're the first company purpose-built  to the deliver portfolios of clean, quiet, load-enabling power over the wires to meet utility BYOC requirements and get data centers connected faster, simpler and cheaper than alternatives like behind-the-meter gas. 

And this week, we're featured in @FastCompany , in an excellent profile written by @adele_peters:

"The U.S. is on track to add a record 86 gigawatts of new wind, solar, and battery storage capacity this year—roughly the size of the U.K.’s entire grid. And there’s far more clean energy in the pipeline, with low-cost proposed projects that could help meet the surging demand from data centers. So why are data centers increasingly turning to polluting gas plants instead of clean energy?

A startup called Firma Power says that the issue isn’t cost, speed, or reliability, but the difficulty of assembling enough clean energy from a patchwork of projects—a problem that it is trying to solve.

Securing enough reliable, clean electricity for a massive new data center is complex. But Firma’s software calculates what a proposed data center needs, and then automatically searches through proposed clean energy projects to suggest a portfolio that could support it. An analysis that might otherwise take a team months can now take minutes. Firma then does the hard work of pulling all of the clean energy projects together, and data center developers can sign a single contract.

The company says that the process can get data centers power faster than building new gas-fired power plants—and it can compete on cost. And at a time when Americans really don’t like data centers, using clean power could make it more feasible for some projects to be greenlit by communities."

article.plain_text:
Additional funding will help states, territories, and tribes modernize critical energy infrastructure, improve grid reliability, and deliver more affordable electricity to American families and businesses.
WASHINGTON— The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) today announced approximately $967 million in additional funding through its Grid Resilience State and Tribal Formula Grant program to modernize critical energy infrastructure, lower electricity costs and strengthen America’s power grid. The funding will support locally driven projects across states, territories, and tribes to upgrade critical infrastructure, prevent power disruptions, and meet growing electricity demand while helping lower costs for American families and businesses.
The investment advances President Trump’s American energy dominance agenda. Projects funded through the program will help states, territories, and tribes invest in infrastructure improvements that protect against disruptive events, improve system performance, and ensure communities and businesses have dependable power when they need it most.
“Lowering costs and unleashing prosperity are top priorities for President Trump,” said U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright. “These commonsense investments provide resources directly to states, territories, and tribes to lower electricity costs and strengthen grid reliability for American businesses and families.”
“A strong and dependable grid is the backbone of American economic prosperity,” said Office of Electricity Assistant Secretary Katie Jereza. “This funding will help Americans across the country, including our tribal partners, optimize their electricity systems and prepare for future growth while strengthening energy security and deploying technologies that can lower the long-term cost of delivering reliable power.”
States, tribes, and U.S. territories can view their funding allocations and application instructions here.

At the peak of the HIV epidemic, AIDS caused more than half of all deaths in some countries.

The HIV epidemic — which started in the early 1980s and progressed rapidly in the 1990s — has had lasting impacts that continue today. More than 800,000 people still die from HIV/AIDS every year.

But some countries were hit much harder than others.

In the chart, you can see the share of all deaths in a given year caused by HIV/AIDS in four countries that were particularly badly affected.

At the height of the epidemic, more than half of all deaths in Zimbabwe and Botswana, and over 40% in South Africa and Namibia, were caused by the disease.

Thankfully, interventions to prevent the spread of HIV and treatments such as antiretroviral therapy have reduced death rates across the world. But about one in five deaths in these countries was still caused by AIDS in 2023.

(written by @_HannahRitchie and @parriagadap)

note_tweet.text:
One VERY cool thing @PeterRFB and I did for our new @FamStudies report was survey people about the celebrities they admired.

But.... that got us curious!

What was the real general fertility behavior of social and cultural elites? How would we know?

To assess this, we scraped every person off of Wikipedia and Wikidata back to 1500 for some countries of interest, then triaged down to those with relatively credible actual family data. This yields literally hundreds of thousands of people with demographic data. In general we suspect the estimates for elite fertility are too low; probably about 30% too low around 1800, and probably about 5-10% too low today, with drift between those values, but we have chosen not to make arbitrary corrections.

Rather than keep it to ourselves, we've posted it as an interactive tool you can browse here: https://t.co/qQeGioYnpN

The results are pretty interesting. For example, in one of the figures below, you can see Israeli vs. Egyptian elites over time. Israeli elite family size was diverging from Egyptian perhaps by 1940, but no later than 1985! This is pretty fascinating since national fertility rates didn't actually flip in favor of Israel until the 2010s!!

Maybe you're interested in types of elites? We got you covered! In the figures I show data for the UK for selected types of elites. Arts/cultural/musical elites always had fewer kids than business/political/athletic elites; same story for scientific elites. Interesting, ya?

Anyways, you can explore the tool yourself! It's pretty cool!

Full report is here: https://t.co/wcTbqrPNol

The difficulty of this whole case is, of course, that the case itself is sealed-- a grand jury case involving a minor!

And that, ultimately, while he was charged he was not convicted. Maybe he would have been had he not skipped town.

But of course, "CPS took custody away" isn't very dispositive, since we all know CPS takes custody away on the basis of serious allegations as a precaution, and does not require much evidentiary basis to do so (and that's not unreasonable).

Doesn't make Vivek's ad a good call, but people seem to be taking for granted that Amy's stepfather actually raped her, and that fact, to the best of my knowledge, is not actually established, much like the "we lived in a tent" claim may not be. The brother's testimony unfortunately also isn't dispositive; two estranged children disliking their mom is not implausible.

This is why in general I resent it when candidates make their messy personal story part of their political platform-- the facts here are super murky! Nobody should want to be prying into either side of this for political gain! The whole thing is gross!

note_tweet.text:
In this new report, @lymanstoneky @PeterRFB and @DrJasonCarroll begin the work of opening the black box of fertility culture. We explore the specific factors across and within societies that lead some people to have many more children than others.

We used a survey of nearly 10,000 people spanning over a dozen countries.
Most of our survey covered questions that have rarely, if ever, been
surveyed cross-nationally, or have not been surveyed in a research program that also. As a result, we can present first-of-a-kind evidence on what specific. cultural norms typify successful pronatal cultures.

Here are our main findings:

1. Friends and family matter to fertility intentions.

2. The family lives of celebrities (and the visibility of celebrity family lives)
influence the family lives of fans.

3. Effective pronatal beliefs entail positive attitudes towards family life, but not necessarily any particular sense of obligation.

4. Division of household labor does not have a big impact on fertility.

5. Active faith matters to fertility desire and outcomes.

6. A willingness to take risks and an optimism about the future both predict intentions to have children and the number of children a respondent already has.
